extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political philosophy; readers of Montesquieu
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical critique of Montesquieu's classification of governments (republic, monarchy, despotism), his claimed constitutive and conservative principles, and how those ideas explain persistence and corruption of regimes. The page explicates, defends, and criticizes Montesquieu's notions (virtue, honor, moderation, fear, opinion) with historical examples and theoretical refinements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as the principle of republics
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu's maxim: 'la vertu est le principe des républiques' — the republic rests on political virtue rather than purely moral or Christian virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political virtue is defined as love of the fatherland and of equality (the 'virtù politique'); it is the motor that animates republican government and the necessary conservative principle for democracies. If the people lack virtue, excessive liberty leads to division, vice, and eventual collapse; democracy in particular 'ne vit que par la vertu.' Examples/notes: virtue here means obedience to laws, respect for magistrates, love of country, justice; loss of virtue leads to corruption and degeneration toward aristocracy or despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political virtue defined (love of patria and equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Political virtue is explicitly distinguished from moral/Christian virtue: it is 'l'amour de la patrie, c'est-à-dire l'amour de l'égalité.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition explains why virtue functions differently in different regimes: it is a collective civic disposition (esteem for equality and the common good) that sustains democratic institutions. The text emphasizes the difference between possessing such virtue and it being the active 'ressort' of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor as the principle of monarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu posits 'l'honneur' (the prejudice/opinion of each person and condition) as the conservative principle that keeps monarchy from sliding into despotism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honor functions as a social set of expectations and distinctions (preference for rank, prestige) that make both prince and elites sensitive to reputation and thus to limits on arbitrary power. The critic notes ambiguity in Montesquieu's use: honor can mean vanity/ambition or dignity/grandeur of soul; in the latter sense it serves as a restraint, tempering obedience by a sense of what one owes oneself as well as to the sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation as the principle of aristocracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu associates 'la modération' with the aristocracy: a disposition among nobles to regard themselves as equal and thus to moderate their domination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderation preserves aristocratic regimes by restraining nobles' passions and preventing oppression of the people. The critic points out limitations: moderation is better seen as a limiting condition necessary to all governments rather than a specific active principle of aristocracy; it prevents extremes but does not itself generate political motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear as the principle of despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Despotism 'ne repose que sur la crainte' — the sole principle of despotism is fear of the sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fear both restrains the populace and is invoked as the protection of the weak against the great. The critic explains that this leads to silence rather than genuine peace, and that despotism lacks a constitution or stable structure because it depends on arbitrary will rather than law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between constitutive and conservator principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A government has a constitutive principle (what makes it be) and a conservator principle (what makes it endure); e.g., love of liberty/rest vs virtue/honor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This analytical distinction is central: constitutive principles (love of liberty for democracy, love of rest for monarchy) explain why a form arises; conservator principles (virtue for republics, honor/opinion for monarchies) explain durability. The critic uses this distinction to evaluate Montesquieu's claims and to propose refinements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of sovereignty as basis for classifying governments (one/few/all)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classifying governments by who holds sovereignty—one, several, or all—(and whether they obey laws) is a foundational criterion (Aristotelian scheme).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic argues that Montesquieu mixes this distribution principle with the obedience-to-law principle, producing confusion between three versus six types. He recommends consistent classification either by obedience to laws first (good/bad triplet for 3 forms each) or by number (one/several/all) with subdivisions. Practical implication: clarity in taxonomy requires not mixing different classificatory axes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of intermediary powers and privileges in monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Monarchy requires intermediary powers (nobility, clergy, towns, seigneurial/jurisdictional privileges) which serve as channels and limits on the prince's power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These intermediate bodies make the monarch dependent on established customs and institutions, announcing and recalling laws; removing them risks turning monarchy into despotism or popular rule. The critic stresses that monarchy without such organs tends toward arbitrary rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of laws and a 'deposit of laws' for constitutional memory
rubrics_metrics.description: A deposit of laws and a political body to promulgate and recall laws are necessary so the limits of monarchical authority remain present to prince and subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without durable legal repositories and bodies to publicize laws, the prince can rule by whim. Laws are described as conditions of monarchy; their institutional preservation prevents arbitrary change and maintains continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problematic sharp divide between monarchy and despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic challenges Montesquieu's rigid separation of monarchy (law-limited) and despotism (no laws), arguing absolute monarchs can in law change laws and despotisms often have customary limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion cautions against assuming essential differences where degrees exist; in practice a continuum exists and institutional protections (powers guaranteeing laws) are what distinguish a limited monarchy from despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruption begins with corruption of principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The corruption of each government 'commence toujours par celle des principes' — regime decay starts when its guiding principle decays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a diagnostic criterion: watch for the erosion of the constitutive or conservator principle (virtue, honor, moderation, fear) to predict regime degeneration. Examples: democracy loses spirit of equality or exaggerates it; aristocracy when nobles separate from people; monarchy when honor becomes servitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy corruption by loss or exaggeration of equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy perishes either by losing its spirit of equality or by exaggerating it (making equality extend to magistrates, fathers, husbands), which destroys necessary social bonds and respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two failure modes: 1) loss of equality → oligarchy/aristocracy; 2) excessive equality → demagoguery, general despotism then single tyrant. The page cites classical sources (Plato) and warns that extreme liberty without virtue leads to small tyrants and eventual complete loss of freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy corrupts when nobles detach from people or command without law
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristocracy is corrupted when the nobility ceases to be united with the people, no longer commands via laws/justice, or when power centralizes among nobles becoming tyrannical or weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators: nobles relish command more than its perils, feel secure from consequences. The result is tyranny or impotence. Preservation requires nobles' connection to the people and rule by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy corrupts when honor turns to servitude and laws are replaced by will
rubrics_metrics.description: Monarchy decays when honor degenerates into servility, when subjects (including grands) become instruments of the prince, when honors and infamy coexist, and when the monarch replaces laws with will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs of corruption include suppression of intermediate powers, replacement of justice by severity, and the prince's love of caprice over legitimate will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotism is inherently corrupt and lacks constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Despotism, being founded solely on one will and fear, 'ne peut avoir rien de déterminé et d'assuré; il n'a donc point de constitution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion implies that systems resting on arbitrary will cannot form stable constitutional orders: they produce silence, not genuine peace, and are self-contradictory because fear undermines security. Historical comparisons used (Caracalla, Heliogabalus) and orientalist examples questioned as caricatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of rest vs love of liberty as constitutive human principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Two natural human principles underlie the two main forms: love of rest (leads to monarchy) and love of liberty (leads to democracy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This anthropological criterion explains citizens' dispositions: those preferring rest avoid public affairs and accept orderly rule; those loving liberty crave participation, equality, and constant debate. The disposition of the populace predicts the likely constitutional form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion/public opinion as a conservative principle in monarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: In monarchies there exists an 'opinion'—a public sense that the king owes the happiness of subjects—which, though less free than in democracies, exerts influence on princes and ministers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strength of public opinion is a measure: a living opinion restrains monarchic arbitrariness; weak opinion signals drift toward despotism. Opinion is distinct from honor (opinion is more democratic; honor more aristocratic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation is a general preservative, not a unique aristocratic principle
rubrics_metrics.description: While Montesquieu assigns moderation to aristocracy, the critic argues moderation is a limit necessary to all governments to avoid extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should not treat moderation as an internal motor of aristocracy but as a cross-cutting condition: monarchy without moderation → despotism; democracy without moderation → demagogy/tyranny. Thus moderation is diagnostic of regime health rather than a genre-defining principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor is ambiguous and must be specified (vanity vs dignity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu's notion of honor mixes meanings: 'prejudice of each person and condition', vanity/ambition, and elements of virtue (nobility, frankness, politeness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical caution: when using 'honor' as a criterion, specify whether it means aristocratic prestige (which can limit princely power) or vanity/ambition (which can fuel despotism). Properly defined, honor can be a restraint when it entails refusing dishonorable commands and upholding dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification must not mix axes (obedience-to-law vs number-of-rulers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic objects to Montesquieu's mixing of two classification principles (distribution of sovereignty and obedience to laws), arguing taxonomy should be coherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For evaluative clarity, choose one classificatory axis consistently (either who rules: one/several/all, then subdivide by law-respecting vs arbitrary; or first whether government obeys laws, then subdivide by number). Mixing yields conceptual confusion about whether monarchy and despotism are distinct kinds or degrees.
